analysis.one_liner: Lets federal land plans stand even when a species becomes endangered or new science emerges, without a fresh wildlife review.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a hearing or a vote, so the current requirement for renewed Endangered Species Act reviews stayed on the books.
analysis.plain_summary: Under the Endangered Species Act, when a species is newly listed as threatened or endangered, or when new information about a species comes to light, federal agencies must take a fresh look — a new "consultation" — at how their land management plans affect it. The FIR Act would have eliminated that requirement for Forest Service and Bureau of Land Management plans: once a plan was approved, it could stay in place with no renewed wildlife review, even as species declined. The practical effect is that logging, grazing, and mining approved under an old plan could continue even when new science shows it is pushing a listed species toward extinction. The bill never received a hearing or a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Companies and operators who use federal land for logging, grazing, and mining would gain, because their approved plans could keep going without interruption when a species is newly listed or new science shows harm. Under the Endangered Species Act, a reinitiated consultation can force changes to a plan — reduced logging acreage, seasonal grazing limits, or buffers around critical habitat. This bill would end that risk for plans already approved, amended, or revised, so operators would get more certainty and fewer delays even as wildlife conditions change.

how_it_helps.text: It says neither the Department of Agriculture (which runs the Forest Service) nor the Department of the Interior (which runs the Bureau of Land Management) has to restart consultation when a species is newly listed, critical habitat is designated, or new information about a listed species becomes available.

It writes this rule into the laws governing both Forest Service land management plans and Bureau of Land Management land use plans, overriding the Endangered Species Act consultation requirement for those plans.

analysis.who_pays: Endangered and threatened species and the public that owns the federal lands would bear the cost. Without a required fresh look, plans written years earlier — based on information now outdated — could keep authorizing logging, grazing, or mining even when new evidence shows they are harming a species that was healthy or unknown when the plan was approved. Citizens would lose their main legal tool for forcing the government to reexamine those plans.
analysis.who_pays_short: Endangered species and public land users

drawbacks.text: The bill would leave land management plans in place even when a species is newly listed as threatened or endangered or new science shows its habitat is being harmed, so harmful logging, grazing, or mining authorized under an old plan could continue without a fresh look. Once a plan was approved, there would be no trigger for a second review, which weakens the main safety valve in Endangered Species Act consultations.

The bill does not ban reconsultation outright — the agencies could still choose to consult voluntarily — but by removing the legal requirement it removes the only lever citizens and conservation groups can use to force a reexamination when a plan is hurting a listed species.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered a real benefit to logging, grazing, and mining operators on federal land: fewer review delays. But the cost fell on species with no voice in the process — plans written years ago would keep governing land even after new science showed a listed species was being harmed, and the public would have no straightforward way to force a second look. Since the agencies would still have discretion to reconsult voluntarily, the bill would have mainly removed the legal pressure that makes them do it. The one-sidedness of the trade — a targeted industry gain paid for by weakened wildlife safeguards on land owned by everyone — is the honest bottom line.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to the House Natural Resources and Agriculture Committees, then split among three subcommittees, and no committee ever took it up before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Matt Rosendale of Montana introduced the FIR Act on February 18, 2021, with nine Republican cosponsors.

The House referred it to the Natural Resources and Agriculture Committees the same day, and in late March 2021 split it among three subcommittees: National Parks, Forests, and Public Lands; Water, Oceans, and Wildlife; and Conservation and Forestry.
No hearing, markup, or floor vote ever appears in the action history, and the Congress ended on January 3, 2023, so the bill expired.

Under current law, as described in the bill's own summary, agencies must reconsult when a species is listed, critical habitat is designated, or new information about a species emerges; because the bill never became law, that requirement remains in place.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died, the existing rule that federal agencies must take a fresh look at land plans when a species becomes endangered or new science arrives stayed intact, protecting endangered wildlife on national forests and public lands. The logging, grazing, and mining interests the bill was written for did not get the exemption they wanted.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Endangered wildlife and public lands; industry did not

for.name: Rep. Matt Rosendale
for.what_they_did: Introduced the FIR Act to end mandatory reconsultation on Forest Service and Bureau of Land Management plans.

for.name: 9 Republican cosponsors
for.role: Reps. Westerman, Simpson, Newhouse, Gosar, Fulcher, Baird, LaMalfa, Herrell, and Boebert

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all nine cosponsors were Republicans; no Democrat sponsored or cosponsored the bill, and no member of either party acted to move it or stop it on the record — it simply died in committee.

industries.industry: Timber and logging companies operating on federal forests
industries.note: Cutting plans approved years ago could keep going without a new endangered species review when a species is newly listed or new science arrives, meaning fewer stoppages and delays on national forest timber sales. Ordinary people bear the cost in reduced protection for wildlife on public land.

industries.industry: Livestock ranchers grazing on federal land
industries.note: Grazing permits tied to Bureau of Land Management and Forest Service plans would be harder to disturb by a new endangered species finding, reducing the chance that grazing would be curtailed for a listed species. The cost falls on wildlife and the public land users who value it.

industries.industry: Mining and energy developers on federal public lands
industries.note: Land use plans that open areas to mining, oil, and gas development could not be forced back into consultation when new information about a listed species emerges, protecting approved projects from interruption. The public pays with weaker safeguards for the wildlife on its own land.
